title: Chunky toy low-poly: rounded blocks, big heads, soft light
text: A friendly low-poly look with chunky proportions, very few facets and soft ambient light. Reads as safe and playful for kids, and big shapes stay legible in a headset at 2-5 m. Ready prompt_style: "chunky toy-like low-poly, rounded blocky shapes, big-headed cute characters, soft ambient light, gentle shadows, bright cheerful mood".
use_when: Kids, families, toy, candy or farm themes
do: Copy the prompt_style line into art.prompt_style
Pair with candy, toy or farm palettes
avoid: Thin spiky details that break the toy feel

title: Heroic fantasy low-poly: sharp facets, rim light, epic scale
text: Sharper facets, taller silhouettes and a warm rim light give a heroic, adventure feel. Good for battle and boss moments where the enemy should feel big. Ready prompt_style: "heroic fantasy low-poly, sharp angular facets, strong warm rim light, dramatic scale, epic adventure mood".
use_when: Battle games, boss fights, knights, dragons, teens and gamers
do: Copy the prompt_style line into art.prompt_style
Make the boss 2-3 times player height in key art
avoid: Gritty realism or gore

title: Diorama tabletop low-poly: tilt-shift, clean board, miniature feel
text: Looks like a painted miniature game on a table. Ideal for tactics, where the board must read as a grid of squares and the pieces as figurines. Ready prompt_style: "miniature diorama low-poly, clean tabletop board, figurine-like pieces, soft tilt-shift depth of field, crisp grid".
use_when: Tactics boards, puzzle games, top-down presentation
do: Copy the prompt_style line into art.prompt_style
Keep the board fully in frame
avoid: Heavy fog or bloom that hides squares

title: Spooky-cute low-poly: big eyes, purple shadows, warm windows

avoid: All-white frames in daylight

title: Art style is always stylized low-poly, flat shaded: vary mood, not technique
text: Every FortalLand game uses the same 1,900+ low-poly flat-shaded models, so the prototype art must promise exactly that. Vary the mood with palette, lighting preset and silhouette size, never with realistic, painted, pixel or anime styles that the build cannot match.
use_when: Writing art.style and art.prompt_style for any prototype
do: Start art.style with "low-poly" in lang
Describe mood words: cozy, eerie, epic, festive
Name the lighting preset you expect (noon, evening, spooky, neon)
avoid: "Realistic", "photoreal", "cel-shaded anime", "pixel art" in prompt_style
Promising textures or detail the catalog lacks

title: MR key art: first-person through the headset, real room visible, only the floor changed
text: For MR the honest key art is the player view: a real room (walls, windows, people) with the game floor replacing only the real floor and low-poly objects standing on it. The code already adds the MR view line, so the prompt should describe the real room concretely (a school hall with windows, a living room sofa at the edge).
use_when: key_art.prompt for any MR game
do: Name 2 real room details from the brief environment
Put the game objects at 1-4 m distance on the floor
Include a hand or controller at the bottom edge only if needed, kept simple
avoid: Virtual sky, walls or ceilings replacing the real room
Showing the player flying or running

title: MR alternative: over-the-shoulder of a player in the real room
text: A third-person shot of a person wearing a headset in the real space, with the virtual floor and objects drawn around them, explains MR to people who have never tried it. Use it when the brief stresses spectators or families watching.
use_when: MR games for events, first-time VR players, or where the creator must pitch to others
do: Show one player from behind at waist height, 2-3 m away
Show spectators at the edge of the frame, outside the play area
avoid: More than 2 players in frame, FLUX blends faces and limbs
Visible text on the headset

see_also.why: Reeves et al. specifically address designing for spectators who watch players perform in public, including how to make the player's experience visible and understandable to onlookers.

title: PC battle key art: low third-person behind the hero mid-combo
text: Camera 2-3 m behind and slightly above the sword hero, the boss or a beast charging in from the far side, a red warning ring on the ground between them. One clear action pose (sword swing or dash) sells the 3-hit combo and dash in one frame.
use_when: key_art.prompt for a PC battle game
do: Describe one hero, one big enemy and at most 3 small grunts in the distance
Name the theme ground (ice, lava, forest)
avoid: Crowds of enemies, FLUX merges them into mush
Guns, bows or magic bolts the engine lacks

title: MR battle key art: player view, controller as sword, enemies walking in from the room edge
text: Show the player view in the real room: a low-poly sword where the right controller would be, 2-3 grunts or a shield enemy walking slowly in from the wall side, a red ring glowing at the player's feet. This is exactly what the MR battle engine does, so the picture does not overpromise.
use_when: key_art.prompt for an MR battle game
do: Enemies 2-4 m away at the real floor edge
Red ring near the bottom of the frame
avoid: Enemies jumping from the ceiling or walls
Player running or leaping

title: Tactics key art: high three-quarter view of the whole 6 x 8 board
text: A board game sells through its board. Use a high 45-60 degree view showing the whole board, the player piece (knight, rook...) as a large figurine, 1-2 guard pieces and a glowing target square. In MR show the board lying on the real floor of the room.
use_when: key_art.prompt for a tactics game on PC or MR
do: Say "6 by 8 checkered board seen from a high angle"
Name the player piece type
One target clearly highlighted
avoid: Close-ups where the grid is not visible
Asking FLUX for exact square counts; accept roughly a board

title: Runner key art: looking down the route toward the portal
text: Put the camera at walking height looking along the route: a checkpoint marker close, one red hazard circle on the path, and the glowing portal at the far end framed by theme scenery. The eye travels the route the way the player will.
use_when: key_art.prompt for a runner on PC or MR
do: One leading line (path) from bottom to the portal
One hazard and one checkpoint, no more
avoid: A route shown from too high, it reads as a map not a game
Many hazards that make it look impossible

title: Pick the climax moment, not the start screen
text: Only one picture is drawn, so draw the storyboard climax: the boss turning, the last target captured, the portal opening. A start-of-game picture looks empty and sells nothing.
use_when: Choosing what key_art.prompt shows
do: Copy the climax panel action into the prompt
Write the caption as a short exciting line in lang
avoid: Menus, title cards or lobby scenes
The quiet tutorial area

title: FLUX schnell draws text, hands and crowds badly: design around them
text: FLUX schnell is fast but garbles letters, fuses fingers and melts groups of more than 2-3 characters. Keep prompts to one hero subject, few secondary shapes, no readable signs, and hands either hidden or holding a simple object.
use_when: Writing any key_art.prompt
do: Max 1 main character and 3 minor ones
Say "blank sign" or omit signs
Use big simple props instead of detailed hands
avoid: Scoreboards, banners with words, logos
Close-up hands, dancing groups, crowds

title: Key art prompt order: camera, subject, action, setting, light
text: The code appends the view, the low-poly style and the palette, so the prompt itself should be 1-3 sentences in this order: camera angle, main subject, what happens, setting, light. 40-90 English words is enough; longer prompts dilute the subject.
use_when: Writing key_art.prompt text
do: Example: "Low angle behind a small knight, a giant ice beast charges across a frozen arena, a red warning ring glows between them, cold blue dusk light."
avoid: Repeating the style or palette (code adds it)
Thai words in the prompt, it is checked and rejected

title: No HUD, score or words in the key art
text: The picture is an in-game moment without interface, so health bars, timers and titles stay out of key_art.prompt. HUD is listed separately in hud. Words in the prompt make FLUX draw fake letters, which look broken and cannot be translated.
use_when: Any key art that mentions score, timers or titles
do: Describe the HUD in hud only
Convey score with visual objects (a glowing target, a portal)
avoid: "with the title FortalLand at the top"
"score 300 shown"

title: MR key art must not replace the real walls or sky
text: Only the floor changes in MR, so a key art with a fantasy sky or castle walls around the player promises something the headset will never show. Big scenery should stand on the floor and be lower than the real room, or be marked VR only.
use_when: MR prototypes with grand themes (castle, space, ocean)
do: Put towers or trees on the floor inside the room
Let the real ceiling or sky stay visible
avoid: Full fantasy skyboxes
Underwater fog filling the whole room

title: Titles: 1-3 words, sayable in Thai and English, one concrete image
text: A good title is short enough to shout across a venue and names one concrete thing: "Lantern Run", "Naga Gate", "Ice Knight". Thai players should be able to say the English or the Thai version without awkward sounds. Avoid generic words like "Adventure", "Quest", "World" on their own.
use_when: Writing prototype.title
do: Noun + verb or adjective + noun
Check it is under 16 characters
Offer a Thai form that keeps the same image
avoid: "Super Fun Adventure Game"
Puns that only work in one language
Brand names you do not own

title: Title examples that work bilingually
text: Examples: "Krathong Glow", "Ghost Market Dash", "Knight of Ice", "Tuk-Tuk Rush", "Dino Steps", "Temple Chess". Each names the theme and hints at the verb in 2-3 words.
use_when: Needing inspiration for a title in th or en
do: Mirror the core loop verb (dash, steps, guard, catch)
avoid: Copying existing game or film titles

title: Logline: you are X, you do Y, because Z is fun
text: One sentence: who the player is, what they physically do, and the hook. "You are the last lantern keeper, walking the night river to relight 6 krathongs before the ghosts drift in." It must describe the real verb of the genre (walk, step out of rings, swing, move like a knight).
use_when: Writing prototype.logline
do: Include a number (6 lanterns, 3 chapters, 90 seconds)
Use the genre verb
avoid: Abstract taglines ("an unforgettable journey")
Verbs the engine lacks (shoot, build, talk)

title: Pillars must be testable choices, not adjectives
text: A pillar is a rule every part must serve, so it must be able to reject ideas. "Every danger is seen 2 seconds before it hits" rejects instant traps; "Fun and exciting" rejects nothing. Write 3 pillars: one for feeling, one for play, one for the real space or players.
use_when: Writing the 3 prototype.pillars
do: Good: "Kids can finish without reading"
Good: "Spectators see every big moment"
Good: "Always one step from safety"
avoid: Vague: "Beautiful graphics", "Immersive", "Fun for everyone"
3 pillars that all say the same thing
source: Schell, The Art of Game Design

title: Derive one pillar from each top MDA feeling in the brief
text: Map the brief feelings to concrete pillars: challenge becomes "Fail fast, retry in 3 seconds"; fellowship becomes "Friends race side by side and see each other"; discovery becomes "Every checkpoint reveals a new view"; submission becomes "No way to lose, only to be faster"; narrative becomes "Each checkpoint is one line of the story".
use_when: Turning brief.feelings into pillars
do: Keep the MDA word out of the pillar, write the behaviour
avoid: Pillars unrelated to the brief feelings

title: Battle storyboard: first wave, mixed wave, boss, victory
text: Start: 2-3 slow grunts walk in, the player learns to swing. Middle: a shield enemy plus grunts, the player must hit from the side, rain rings fall. Climax: the boss or beast charges, the player steps out of a red ring and lands the combo. End: the arena calms, score and time shown.
use_when: Writing storyboard panels for a battle game
do: player_does in MR: swing, turn, step out of a ring
player_does on PC: 3-hit combo, dash
avoid: A beast in the first chapter (checked)
MR players running or dodging by sprinting

title: Tactics storyboard: read the board, first capture, beat the guards, last target
text: Start: the player sees the board, their piece and 1-2 guards, and plans the first move. Middle: they capture targets in order while counting guard beats. Climax: the last target sits next to an attacked square and must be taken on the right beat. End: the board clears, time goes on the leaderboard.
use_when: Writing storyboard panels for a tactics game
do: player_does in MR: walk onto a square
Mention the piece type in every panel
avoid: More than 2 guards on board 1 (checked)
Real-time chasing, guards move on a beat of 3 s or slower

title: Runner storyboard: spawn view, first hazard, final stretch, portal
text: Start: the player sees the first checkpoint and the story card. Middle: hazards appear between checkpoints, touching one sends them back. Climax: the last checkpoint and the most dramatic view (void drop, big creature). End: the portal, the score with time bonus.
use_when: Writing storyboard panels for a runner
do: Tie each panel to a checkpoint label
player_does: walk to, step around, touch
avoid: Jumping, climbing or collecting items
Climax in a corner spectators cannot see

title: player_does uses the body verb, not the story verb
text: Captions tell the story ("The ghost queen wakes"); player_does says what the body does ("steps left out of the red ring and swings twice"). Creators judge buildability from player_does, so keep it physical and possible.
use_when: Filling storyboard[].player_does
do: MR: walk, turn, step, swing, stop
PC: move with WASD, click to attack, dash
avoid: "Defeats the queen" without saying how
Verbs like shoot, pick up, talk

title: Use 3 panels for 2-3 minute games, 4 for longer
text: Short sessions have no real middle: start, climax, end is honest. Games of 4 minutes or more need a middle panel to show the twist or difficulty step. Each panel needs its own beat and one must be the climax.
use_when: Deciding storyboard length
do: 3 panels: start, climax, end
4 panels: start, middle, climax, end
avoid: Two middle panels or no climax (checked)

title: In MR put the climax where the audience can see it
text: Spectators see bodies, not the game, so the climax should be a big body action (turning to face the boss, a wide step out of a ring, walking through the portal) placed on the side nearest the audience zone.
use_when: MR storyboards with spectators in the brief
do: Say in the caption where the audience is
Match the climax position to the sketch zone
avoid: Climax in the far corner
Tiny hand-only actions at the climax

see_also.why: Reeves et al. discuss how spectators see the player's body and manipulations rather than the game state, so performances should be designed with audience visibility in mind.

title: Battle HUD: health, chapter, enemies left, score
text: A battle player needs four facts: how much health is left, which chapter of how many, how many enemies remain, and the score. On PC add a dash cooldown. Keep it to 4-5 items.
use_when: Writing hud for a battle game
do: Health hearts or bar
Chapter 2/4
Enemies left
Score
avoid: Mana, ammo or inventory slots the engine lacks

title: Tactics HUD: board number, targets captured, guard beat, timer
text: Tactics play is planning on a beat, so the HUD shows the board (1/5), captured targets in order (2/4), a guard beat indicator that ticks before guards move, and the race timer for the leaderboard.
use_when: Writing hud for a tactics game
do: Board 1/5
Targets 2/4 in order
Guard beat ring
Timer
avoid: Move history lists or text-heavy hints

title: Runner HUD: checkpoint count, score, timer, next label
text: The runner engine tracks checkpoints in order, score (+100 checkpoint, -25 hazard, +300 finish) and optional time limit. Show checkpoint 3/6, the next checkpoint label as the story line, score and timer. In a race add live position.
use_when: Writing hud for a runner
do: Checkpoint 3/6
Next: "Feed the dragon"
Score
Timer or time left
avoid: Lives counters, the engine resets to the last checkpoint instead

title: Kids HUD: 2 items, icons not numbers
text: For players under 9, show at most 2 HUD items as icons: progress (lit lanterns 3 of 6) and one danger cue. Numbers, timers and scores can live on the spectator screen for parents instead.
use_when: hud when the brief players are young kids
do: Progress as icons
Move score to the end screen
avoid: Timers counting down for small kids
Text instructions in the HUD

title: MR HUD stays low and few: nothing that needs looking up while walking
text: In passthrough the HUD floats in view, so keep it to 2-4 items near the lower edge or on the wrist. Players walking must keep their eyes on the floor. Big messages appear only when the player is standing still (start, chapter break, end).
use_when: MR hud lists
do: 2-4 items
Flash major info at stops
avoid: Long text, minimaps, top-of-view elements
source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

title: Runner flow, 2 minutes, 5 checkpoints
text: 0:00 story card and first view. 0:10 checkpoint 1, an easy straight. 0:30 first hazard pair. 0:50 checkpoint 3 with the best view. 1:20 tight zig-zag hazard. 1:40 last checkpoint. 1:50 portal and score. Short loops suit spaces under 4 x 4 m.
use_when: Runner sessions of 2 minutes or small MR spaces
do: About 20 s between checkpoints
avoid: More than 6 checkpoints in 2 minutes

title: Runner flow, 5 minutes, 8 checkpoints with a twist
text: 0:00 intro card. 0:15 checkpoints 1-2 teach hazards. 1:30 checkpoint 3, story turn. 2:30 checkpoints 4-5, denser hazards. 3:30 the dramatic view (void floor section or big creature). 4:20 checkpoint 8. 4:40 portal, score and time bonus. 4:50 leaderboard.
use_when: Runner sessions of 4-6 minutes in medium or large spaces
do: Put a calm stretch after the hardest part
avoid: Same hazard density the whole time

title: Battle flow, 3 minutes, 3 chapters and a boss
text: 0:00 title and stance tip. 0:10 chapter 1: 3 grunts. 0:50 chapter 2: grunts plus a shield. 1:40 chapter 3: rain rings start. 2:20 boss or beast. 2:50 victory and score.
use_when: Battle games in MR or PC around 3 minutes
do: MR: at most 6 enemies per chapter (checked)
5-10 s breather between chapters
avoid: A beast in chapter 1 (checked)

title: Battle flow, 8 minutes, 5 chapters for PC players
text: 0:00 intro. 0:20 ch1 grunts. 1:30 ch2 shields. 2:45 ch3 first beast. 4:00 ch4 rain plus mixed. 5:30 ch5 hard mix up to 9 enemies. 6:45 boss. 7:40 results. Long battles fit PC better than MR, where arms tire after about 4-5 minutes of swinging.
use_when: Long battle sessions, mostly PC gamers
do: Offer a shorter MR variant
avoid: 8-minute MR sword sessions for first-time VR players
source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

title: Tactics flow, 5 minutes, 4 boards
text: 0:00 rules card with the piece moves. 0:20 board 1: 2 targets, 1 guard. 1:20 board 2: 3 targets, 2 guards. 2:40 board 3: new piece, cracked squares. 3:50 board 4: guards on a faster beat. 4:45 time to leaderboard.
use_when: Tactics sessions around 5 minutes
do: Change the piece or one rule per board
avoid: More than 2 guards on board 1 (checked)

title: Tactics flow, 2 minutes, 2 boards for events
text: 0:00 show the knight move on the floor. 0:15 board 1: 2 targets, 1 guard. 1:00 board 2: 3 targets, 2 guards. 1:50 time on the leaderboard. Short and repeatable for queues at events.
use_when: Event booths with queues, first-time players
do: Keep the same piece for both boards
avoid: New rules in the last board of a short session

title: Flow steps every 20-60 seconds, ending with results
text: Write 4-8 flow steps from 0:00 to the end, roughly every 20-60 s, including the intro card at 0:00 and the results or leaderboard as the last step. The last timestamp should match brief.session_minutes within 15 s.
use_when: Writing prototype.flow for any genre
do: Format t as "m:ss"
One sentence per step
avoid: A flow that ends at the climax with no results
Steps longer than 2 minutes

title: First-time VR players: add 15-20 s of standing still at the start
text: People new to headsets need a moment to look around and trust the floor. Start the flow with 15-20 s where nothing threatens them, then introduce the first verb.
use_when: MR flows when brief.vr_experience is low
do: 0:00 look around, 0:15 first task
avoid: Enemies or hazards in the first 10 s
source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

title: Battle sketch: arena with player start in the middle, spawn edges as danger
text: Draw a battle as shape "arena": start at the centre (0.5, 0.5), danger zones at the edges where enemies walk in (r 0.1-0.15), the boss zone on the far side, and the audience zone outside the edge where people stand.
use_when: sketch for any battle game
do: danger at 2-3 edges
audience at y 0.95
avoid: Zones in the centre ring where the player stands

title: Tactics sketch: board shape with start corner and goal on the far side
text: Draw tactics as shape "board": start at a near corner (about 0.2, 0.85), targets as story zones, guards as danger zones, the last target as the goal near the far side. In MR add the audience beside the long edge.
use_when: sketch for any tactics game
do: Use small r (0.05-0.08) so zones look like squares
avoid: A route path; boards do not need one

title: Runner sketch: route with 3-12 path points in walking order
text: Draw a runner as shape "route" with a path of at least 3 points (checked) in walking order, start at the first point, goal (portal) at the last, danger zones on the path between, story zones at key checkpoints. Keep points 0.08 inside the square edge for the 0.6 m safety margin.
use_when: sketch for any runner
do: Loop: return near start
Zig-zag: alternate x 0.2 and 0.8
avoid: Fewer than 3 path points
Path along the very edge of the square

title: MR audience zone sits outside the play area on the side the brief names
text: Put the audience zone where real spectators will be (a long wall, a doorway, chairs), just outside the play area, and bend the route or arena so the climax happens on that side. Never place audience inside the walking area.
use_when: MR sketches when the brief has spectators
do: audience x or y at 0.95-1.0
Climax zone within 0.3 of it
avoid: Audience in the middle of the floor
Hazards right next to the audience edge

see_also.why: Reeves et al. cover designing the spectator experience including the physical relationship between performers and audience in public game settings.

title: PC sketches skip the audience zone
text: On PC spectators watch the screen, so there is no audience place in the level. Use the zones for start, goal or boss, danger and story only.
use_when: sketch for a PC game
do: Spend the zone budget on story spots
avoid: Audience zones on PC levels

title: Sketch with 4-8 zones: one start, one goal or boss, the rest earn their place
text: Up to 10 zones are allowed but 4-8 read best. Every zone kind tells the creator something: start, goal or boss (both required by the check), 1-3 danger, 1-2 story, 1 audience in MR.
use_when: Any prototype sketch
do: Name zones in lang with the story word ("Ghost Gate")
avoid: 10 tiny zones that clutter the plan
Missing start or goal (checked)

title: Small MR room under 4 x 4 m: one loop, big zones
text: In a living room or small classroom the sketch is a tight loop of 4-5 points with large zones (r 0.15-0.25), because a 3 m room only fits about 4 steps per side. Only runner fits below 3 m.
use_when: MR sketches for small spaces
do: Loop path of 4-5 points
avoid: Long zig-zags in tiny rooms
Battle or tactics under 3 x 3 m (checked)

title: Good playtest questions are observable and specific
text: Ask what you can see happen, with a threshold: "Do 4 of 5 first-time players step out of the first red ring within 2 seconds?" Bad questions ask for opinions ("Is it fun?") that players answer politely and that do not tell you what to change.
use_when: Writing prototype.test_questions
do: Name the player group, the moment and a number
One question per pillar
avoid: "Did you like it?"
"Is the art good?"

title: Battle playtest questions
text: Examples: "Do players turn to face enemies coming from behind within 3 seconds?", "How many players get hit by the first rain ring?", "Do MR players stop swinging from arm tiredness before the boss?", "Does the shield enemy make players walk around it?"
use_when: test_questions for battle
do: Watch arm fatigue in MR
avoid: Asking players to rate difficulty 1-10 only

title: Tactics playtest questions
text: Examples: "Can a first-time player say how a knight moves after board 1?", "How many players step on an attacked square on board 2?", "Do players stop and count the guard beat or rush?", "Does anyone walk off the board edge in MR?"
use_when: test_questions for tactics
do: Count mistakes per board
avoid: "Was the puzzle clever?"

title: Runner playtest questions
text: Examples: "Do players find checkpoint 2 without help?", "How many hazards hit per run, and where?", "Do players read the checkpoint labels aloud?", "Does anyone hesitate at the void floor edge longer than 3 seconds?"
use_when: test_questions for runner
do: Mark where hazards hit on the sketch
avoid: "Was the story interesting?"

title: Playtest questions for kids
text: Examples: "Can a 7-year-old finish without an adult explaining?", "Does any child look scared or stop moving at the ghost?", "Do kids point and tell parents what they see?" Watch faces and bodies, kids rarely say they are confused.
use_when: test_questions when players are kids
do: Watch with a parent present
avoid: Asking kids for written feedback

title: Playtest questions for spectators and groups
text: Examples: "Do spectators cheer or call out at the climax?", "Can parents tell who is winning from the leaderboard screen?", "Do waiting players watch or look at phones?" The audience is part of the MR game.
use_when: test_questions when the brief has spectators or a race
do: Observe the audience zone too
avoid: Only questioning the player

see_also.why: Reeves et al. focus on evaluating spectator engagement and experience, matching these playtest questions about audience reactions and involvement.

title: Playtest questions for seniors and first-time VR players
text: Examples: "Does anyone ask to stop in the first minute?", "Do players walk at normal pace or shuffle?", "How many reach for a real wall for balance?" These reveal comfort problems before fun problems.
use_when: test_questions for seniors or first-time VR
do: Note pace and balance
avoid: Long sessions before comfort is checked
source: Meta/Oculus VR comfort and MR design guidelines

title: Bad playtest questions and their good rewrites
text: "Is it too hard?" becomes "How many tries does board 2 take?". "Is the theme cool?" becomes "Do players name the theme without being told?". "Is MR fun?" becomes "Do players look around the room in the first 30 seconds?"
use_when: Reviewing test_questions before sending
do: Rewrite every yes/no opinion into a count or a time
avoid: Leading questions ("Wasn't the boss amazing?")

title: Revising from comments: change only what was asked, keep the rest word for word
text: When the creator comments on a prototype, copy every field they did not mention unchanged and edit only the named parts. Rewriting everything makes them re-review and lose trust that their approved parts survive.
use_when: A prototype request that includes creator comments
do: List mentally which fields the comment touches
Keep title, pillars and palette unless named
avoid: Regenerating the whole prototype
Silently changing the genre

title: Follow the ripple: one change may need its linked fields updated
text: Some comments ripple: "make it night" changes palette, prompt_style and key art light; "add a boss" changes the storyboard climax, the sketch boss zone and the flow; "make it 2 minutes" shortens the flow and may drop the middle panel. Update the linked fields and nothing else.
use_when: Applying a creator comment
do: Map: mood to art and key_art, length to flow and storyboard, place to sketch
avoid: Updating the flow but leaving a 5-minute storyboard

title: When a comment asks for a mechanic the engine lacks, offer the nearest one
text: If the creator asks to "add shooting" or "let them pick up keys", keep the prototype and swap in the closest buildable thing: shooting becomes the sword or stepping out of rings; keys become checkpoints labelled "Key 1, Key 2" in order. Say so kindly in the caption.
use_when: Comments requesting unsupported mechanics
do: Name the replacement in the changed panel
avoid: Promising the mechanic in the key art
Ignoring the comment

title: Change key_art.prompt only when the look or climax changed
text: Each new key art costs a FLUX picture and the creator's attention. Rewrite key_art.prompt when the comment changes the theme, mood, palette, climax or platform; otherwise keep it identical so the same picture can be reused.
use_when: Revisions where the picture may or may not need redrawing
do: Keep the prompt string exactly the same when unchanged
avoid: Tiny wording edits that trigger a redraw

title: Revision example: "too scary for my 6-year-old"
text: Keep title, route and flow. Change art.mood to playful, prompt_style to spooky-cute, palette dark base up one step, key art to a smiling ghost, storyboard climax captions to surprise rather than threat, and add a test question about children stopping in fear.
use_when: Comments that the prototype is too scary
do: Soften the mood fields only
avoid: Removing the theme entirely when they only asked for softer

title: Revision example: "we will play outside at noon now"
text: In MR an outdoor noon venue kills dark and neon looks. Keep the game and story; switch palette to a daylight-safe variant, lighting to noon, remove glow words from prompt_style, and redraw key art with sun and real sky visible. Mention the change in art.mood.
use_when: MR revisions where the venue light changes
do: Raise the darkest palette colour above about #3d5a80
avoid: Keeping a neon palette for noon outdoors

title: Every prototype field must tell the same game
text: Check that the logline verb appears in the storyboard, the climax appears in the key art, the HUD tracks what the flow describes, and the sketch zones match the storyboard places. A creator spots mismatches instantly and stops trusting the plan.
use_when: Final check before replying with a prototype
do: Read logline, climax panel and key art together
avoid: A boss in the storyboard but no boss zone in the sketch

title: Do not let the theme stretch the genre in the prototype
text: A pirate tactics game is still a piece walking a 6 x 8 board; a dragon runner still walks checkpoints and avoids red circles. Theme dresses the engine, it does not add ships to sail or dragons to ride.
use_when: Prototypes with strong themes
do: Describe themed versions of real mechanics (guards as pirate crew)
avoid: Captions promising sailing, flying or riding

title: Battle flow, 2 minutes, MR event version with 2 chapters and a beast
text: 0:00 look around, sword appears in the right hand. 0:15 chapter 1: 3 slow grunts from one wall. 0:50 chapter 2: grunts from two sides plus rain rings. 1:25 a beast charges in as the finale. 1:50 victory and score. Short enough for queues and for arms that tire fast in MR.
use_when: MR battle at events, first-time VR players, sessions of about 2 minutes
do: At most 6 enemies per chapter in MR (checked)
Use the beast only after chapter 1 (checked)
avoid: A full boss fight squeezed into 2 minutes with 4 chapters

title: Battle flow, 3 minutes, PC version with dash taught early
text: 0:00 hero intro and controls. 0:10 chapter 1: 4 grunts, learn the 3-hit combo. 0:45 chapter 2: 2 shields, learn to dash behind them. 1:30 chapter 3: up to 9 mixed enemies with rain. 2:20 boss. 2:50 score and time. PC players tolerate denser chapters than MR players.
use_when: PC battle sessions around 3 minutes
do: Teach one verb per chapter: combo, then dash
avoid: Introducing shields and rain in the same chapter

title: Runner flow, 8 minutes, 10 checkpoints in 3 acts
text: 0:00 story card. 0:20 act 1, checkpoints 1-3, open easy path. 2:30 act 2, checkpoints 4-7, hazard pairs and a story turn at 5. 5:00 calm view stretch, no hazards. 5:45 act 3, checkpoints 8-10, densest hazards or void floor. 7:30 portal. 7:45 score, time bonus, leaderboard. Needs a space over 10 x 10 m or PC.
use_when: Long runner sessions, large venues or PC tours
do: Use the maximum of 10 checkpoints
Plan one rest stretch at mid-session
avoid: 8 minutes in a small room, players loop the same few metres

title: Tactics flow, 8 minutes, 6 boards with a new piece every 2 boards
text: 0:00 rules card. 0:20 boards 1-2 with the rook: 2 then 3 targets, 1-2 guards. 2:30 boards 3-4 with the knight, cracked squares appear. 5:00 boards 5-6 with the queen, guards on a 3 s beat and tables blocking lines. 7:30 final time, leaderboard. Good for puzzle fans on PC or a calm MR hall.
use_when: Long tactics sessions for players who enjoy planning
do: Introduce one new piece or rule every 2 boards
avoid: Guards faster than every 3 s
Six boards of the same piece

title: Classroom learning: chalk green, paper white, pencil yellow, ink blue
text: Palette: #2f5d50 chalk green, #fbfaf5 paper white, #ffcf33 pencil yellow, #2d5bd1 ink blue, #e5262f hazard red. Made for a real classroom under fluorescent light, where everything stays readable. In daylight by windows the paper white can glare, so keep it on small props and use chalk green for the ground. The hazard colour #e5262f (hazard red) is used only for danger so warning rings never blend into the decor.
use_when: Educational games for schools, quiz-style runners where checkpoints are lesson steps
do: Put the 5 hex values straight into art.palette and name them in lang
Scenery theme to pair: ow-library, ow-village
Keep the hazard colour only on danger (rings, enemy tells, cracked squares)
avoid: Adding a second red or orange to the decor, it steals the warning signal

title: Office team-building: slate, teal, warm coral, clean white
text: Palette: #3c4a5c slate, #1fa59a team teal, #ff8a65 warm coral, #f5f7fa clean white, #d7191c hazard red. A calm grown-up palette for meeting rooms and lobbies under office light. Coral is warm but clearly lighter than the hazard red, so keep it on goals and team markers. In daylight it still reads well. The hazard colour #d7191c (hazard red) is used only for danger so warning rings never blend into the decor.
use_when: Corporate team-building, adult groups, office events
do: Put the 5 hex values straight into art.palette and name them in lang
Scenery theme to pair: ow-herotech, ow-garden
Keep the hazard colour only on danger (rings, enemy tells, cracked squares)
avoid: Adding a second red or orange to the decor, it steals the warning signal

title: Tropical beach: lagoon turquoise, white sand, palm green, sunset coral
text: Palette: #23c6c8 lagoon, #f6e7c1 white sand, #3f9b4f palm green, #ff8c69 sunset coral, #7b2cbf urchin purple hazard. Outdoor daylight friendly, like a real beach. Coral and sand are close to warm hazard colours, so hazards turn urchin purple, which stands out on sand and water alike. Indoors raise saturation a step. The hazard colour #7b2cbf (urchin purple hazard) is used only for danger so warning rings never blend into the decor.
use_when: Beach, island holiday, surfing or summer trip themes above water
do: Put the 5 hex values straight into art.palette and name them in lang
Scenery theme to pair: ow-pirate, ow-reef, ow-sun
Keep the hazard colour only on danger (rings, enemy tells, cracked squares)
avoid: Adding a second red or orange to the decor, it steals the warning signal

title: Autumn harvest: maple orange, wheat gold, plum, pine
text: Palette: #d9622b maple orange, #e8c35a wheat gold, #5e2750 plum, #2e5e4e pine, #00b4d8 frost cyan hazard. Warm all over, so a red hazard would hide among leaves; hazards become frost cyan. Pine and plum give the dark anchors. Works indoors and in soft daylight; at noon lift plum toward a lighter berry. The hazard colour #00b4d8 (frost cyan hazard) is used only for danger so warning rings never blend into the decor.

title: Race or shared-floor key art: two players, side by side, one clear leader
text: For an online race or shared floor show exactly 2 player avatars or 2 headset players, one a step ahead, both heading to the same checkpoint or portal. Two figures is the most FLUX schnell draws cleanly, and a visible leader sells competition in one frame.
use_when: key_art.prompt for race or together play modes
do: Give the two players different simple colours (blue and yellow)
Put the goal in the background between them
avoid: 3 or more players, faces and limbs merge
Players touching or passing items, the engine has no hand-offs

title: Together storyboard: shared floor where players see each other, not a team mechanic
text: On a shared floor players walk the same course and see each other's avatars, but there is no shared score or hand-off. Write beats around that: start, players gather at spawn; middle, one waits for or calls out to the other near a hazard; climax, they reach the last checkpoint together; end, both portals and both scores.
use_when: Storyboards for play_mode together
do: Use calling out and waiting as the social verbs
Put both players in the climax panel
avoid: Promising carrying, combining items or team health
A climax only one player can reach

title: Race HUD adds live position; shared-floor HUD adds nothing
text: In a race each player walks their own copy, so add live position (2nd of 4) next to checkpoint count and timer, and mirror the leaderboard on a spectator screen. On a shared floor the other players are visible as avatars, so no extra HUD is needed.
use_when: hud for race or together play modes
do: Race: position, checkpoint 3/6, timer
Shared: the normal runner HUD
avoid: Friend lists, chat or team bars the engine does not have
